content:
I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression.

But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m currently using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer …

The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.

This device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo.

Using one in an Apple Store reinforced both sides of the equation for me.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

What I’m doing now is using the iPhone Duo as my primary phone to discover how those pros and cons balance out in the real world. This first piece is written after just a couple of days, so compromises the things that stand out to me in very early use.

Pros

The large inner display

The size of the inner display is, of course, the whole point of the device: you essentially get an iPad mini that slips into your pocket. As someone who will almost always take a larger display over a smaller one, I do really love this.

When using a single app full screen on the display, it’s significantly more immersive than on other iPhones. For example, it’s normally extremely rare for me to ever watch video on an iPhone screen, but although I would still opt for a MacBook over the iPhone Duo, I have found myself watching more YouTube videos on the device. It does depend to an extent on the aspect ratio of the video, however, with letterboxing reducing the appeal.

It can be a much better way to casually share photos and iPhone videos with other people. I never feel that even a Pro Max screen does justice to most photos, but the iPhone Duo screen can be large enough to do so. This again, however, depends on the aspect ratio. For example, a photo in a 16:9 ratio or similar is actually smaller on this display than it is on a Pro Max.

But a photo with the same aspect ratio as the display, completely filling it, really does look great.

My preference for large screens extends to ebooks, so reading an ebook on an iPhone has always been an absolute last resort. However, while doing so on the Duo certainly wouldn’t be my first choice, it is a significantly better experience than a normal iPhone. I’m currently viewing it as part of my Kindle ecosystem: iPhone Duo, Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Scribe.

Provided an app has been optimized for the display, pretty much everything is just better on this size screen

The anti-reflective coating

While the size may be the headline news, I have to say I’m also a huge fan of the anti-reflective coating. I said when I first tested it that I wished it had also been used on the outer display and was an option on other iPhones, and I’m absolutely still of this view.

It’s almost as if it turns it into a third display type, sitting somewhere between e-ink and conventional glossy screens. I know some find the colors too muted compared to a glossy display, but I don’t find this to be an issue at all. I very much prefer the more paper-like look.

Split view

Split-screen view, positioning one app on each side of the display, is another key feature. The display is too small for windowing, but the split-screen view is very usable for short tasks. It’s especially useful when using two apps simultaneously, such as embedding a photo into a message.

Another handy use is when you’re following instructions in one app to carry out in another – in this case Claude telling me how to transfer an e-SIM from my 18 Pro to the Duo (which it did better than Siri AI <sigh>).

The new gesture of sliding from the bottom of the screen to either the left or right side became instinctive almost immediately – it’s just so obvious. You can also quit either app while leaving the other in place.

Dual-camera view in FaceTime

I had a FaceTime call last night where I was able to let my friend see both my face and what I was looking at. Admittedly, I was mostly using this feature to show off the iPhone Duo itself in a mirror, but I can definitely see situations in which this would be genuinely useful, ranging from tech support to sharing travel experiences.

The outer display usability

The aspect ratio of the outer display definitely takes some getting used to, but you can display the same number of apps as on a standard iPhone. I also found that reachability in one-handed use was better with this than with the iPhone Pro Max, so I view this as a win for the device.

Pocketability

Finally, of course, the other side of the USP of the Duo is the small folded size. The shape is extremely pocketable and fits jeans pockets more comfortably than even a standard iPhone Pro, let alone the Pro Max. At the same time, the increased width is still narrow enough to comfortably fit into a standard jacket/coat inside pocket.

Cons

The camera compromises

I’ve talked about this a lot already as the biggest disincentive for me to buy the Duo, so I’ll just briefly reiterate the key differences here. No telephoto lens*, none of the new Pro controls like variable aperture and shutter speed, no ProRAW photos, no ProRes RAW video.

*This one isn’t huge for me as I mostly shoot in the 0.5 to 2x range, but there are definitely times when longer reach is useful.

The weight

The Duo is heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I have to say that you do feel the weight in one-handed use. While you’re using the outer display, the trade-off is very poor: you’re getting a heavier device with a smaller screen.

When using the inner display, it still feels heavy and isn’t comfortable to hold with one hand, in part due to the lever effect, so I generally hold it with both hands. That’s perfectly usable, with everything within reach of one thumb or the other, and of course the trade-off is very much more reasonable given the size of the display you’re now using.

In my own usage so far, I’ve opened up the phone for anything other than really quick things like checking an incoming message. But if you’re someone who would mostly use the outer screen, as was the case with my colleague Ryan, then I can see why the Duo simply wouldn’t make sense.

The bulk

Closely related to the weight when using the device in folded form, it feels rather bulky, especially with a case on it – and given the extremely high price of a replacement screen, you’d have to be very brave indeed to use it without one!

Touch ID

Perhaps I’ll get used to it, but in the first few days the lack of Face ID has annoyed me Every Single Time I’ve had to unlock the phone or use biometric authentication within an app. Face ID is just so seamless, and Touch ID very much isn’t.

The issue is exacerbated by the fact that the button will be in a different place depending on which way you’re holding the phone, and using it in different orientations is very much more common with the Duo than with a conventional slab iPhone.

The rest-to-unlock setting helps a little, but not much. I’m running it on the developer beta, so I do have Face Unlock enabled, but while I think Apple’s compromises make sense, the practical impact is that it demands Touch ID most of the time.

When I heard the level of complaints being made about the downgrade to Touch ID, I thought people were perhaps making too much fuss about the issue, but even three days in, I have to say I now get it completely.

Unoptimised apps

One of the early adopter pains is unoptimized apps. A lot of them will get fixed quite quickly, I think, but there are always apps that never will – like banking apps. However, this is a smaller issue than I expected it to be.

For example, my development has a concierge app used for things like notifying me when packages have been delivered to the front desk instead of my apartment. With the iPhone Duo unfolded in landscape mode, this app initially opened as a tiny vertical window. However, as soon as I hit the on-screen buttons to flip and resize an unoptimized app, then it became perfectly usable – and it has remembered this setting ever since.

The cost

The final drawback, and a very substantial one, is of course the cost. Yes, it combines the benefits of an iPhone and an iPad mini in one device, but it literally costs the same as buying each of them. Just a few years ago, if you had talked about anyone spending $2,000 plus on a iPhone, it would have seemed absolutely insane. I’m honestly not sure it’s any less insane today.

However, if you do want both devices and would otherwise have bought each of them, then there’s definitely a massive convenience factor in having it all in one pocketable package.

Early conclusions

I said in the intro that there was a definite head versus heart thing going on here. Given the importance of the camera functionality, my head is quite certain that the iPhone 18 Pro is the better device for me. My heart, however, is finding the Duo a dangerously compelling proposition in all other respects.

Top comment by RDLink

I’m where you are. I received mine on Tuesday. It’s too heavy. It’s too expensive, especially with a subpar camera. Touch ID is annoying. The larger screen is going to be rarely used in my day-to-day. Giving up the larger main screen for a screen I’ll rarely use for an extra $1000 seems kinda dumb.

But every so often I open an app or webpage on the larger screen and it’s pretty amazing.

I’ll probably return it. But my choice isn’t the duo or the 18 Pro. By doing away with the iPhone upgrade program and not releasing a pro phone with groundbreaking advancements Apple has removed my incentive to move to the 18. If I send the Duo back I’ll keep my 17 Pro, and see what the Air 2 offers. Much like I moved from the larger, heavier MBP to the smaller, lighter MBA when its power far surpassed what I need I may do the same with my phone if the next gen of the iPhone Air is compelling enough.

My head also wanted to cheat. It proposed that I should carry both devices, using the 18 Pro as a camera and the Duo for everything else. It has taken considerable willpower to reject this idea and leave the 18 Pro at home; that in itself tells its own story.

Even in the first few days, some of the novelty factor has already worn off. For example, that clever blur animation as you unfold the phone is super-cute the first few times you see it, but now I no longer even notice it. The overall excitement of a brand new form factor will similarly wear off over time, though I’m not sure at what rate.

In previous head versus heart battles, I’ve certainly made mistakes in some areas of my life. In the tech sphere, however, my head usually wins out. Right now, then, I have two predictions. First, I’m not going to end up as an iPhone Duo owner. Second, I’m going to be exceedingly sad when I return it.
